title: Metrics and monitoring
problem: Dashboards full of averages and host graphs hide the slow tail, page people on CPU spikes nobody can act on, and fall over when someone adds a user-id label.
summary: Counters, gauges and histograms are the three instruments; RED describes a service and USE a resource. Keep labels bounded, pull rather than push where you can, and page on symptoms users feel rather than on causes.
catTip: I count every mouse I see (counter), weigh myself after dinner (gauge), and sort my naps into buckets by length (histogram). Averaging my nap p99 with the dog's would be nonsense; add the buckets instead.

recall.q: Why can you not average per-instance p99 values to get a service-wide p99, and what should you do instead?
recall.a: A percentile is a position in a distribution, not an additive quantity, so averaging twenty p99s gives a meaningless number. Histogram bucket counts do add: sum each bucket across instances and estimate the quantile from the combined cumulative counts.

guide.breaks: Without the right instruments the team graphs averages that hide the tail, averages percentiles into nonsense, and pages on causes like CPU that nobody can act on at 3 a.m.
guide.tradeoffs: Histograms cost a dozen series per label combination, bounded labels mean you cannot query metrics by user, and symptom-only paging means some causes are found later on a dashboard rather than by a page.
guide.explainSimply: A metric is a number you record over and over: how many requests came in, how many are being handled right now, how long each one took. Think of a car: the odometer only goes up, the speedometer goes up and down, and a tally of journey times sorted into buckets tells you how often a trip was slow. Alerts should work like a smoke alarm, ringing on the smoke rather than on every warm pan.
guide.hint: Ask which quantity you can add across machines: a position in a distribution, or a count of observations in a bucket.

meow: Purr-centiles do not average. Count the naps in each bucket, then meow the p99.

quiz.prompt: You run 20 instances of a service and want the service-wide p99 latency. Which approach is correct?
options: Sum the histogram buckets across instances, then estimate the quantile from the combined buckets
Use the p99 reported by the instance that handles the most traffic
quiz.explanation: Percentiles are positions in a distribution and cannot be averaged or otherwise combined, but bucket counts add, so the fleet-wide quantile is estimated from the summed buckets. The highest per-instance p99 is the strongest distractor: it is an upper bound on the service p99, not the service p99.

quiz.prompt: Which label is most likely to exhaust a Prometheus server's memory?
quiz.explanation: Every unique label combination is a new time series, and a user id is unbounded, so the series count grows with the user base. Status, method and region each have a small, known set of values.

cards.q: A dashboard shows a counter's raw value climbing for days and then dropping to zero. What happened, and how should the panel be written instead?
cards.a: The process restarted, which resets a counter to zero. Graph rate(counter[5m]) rather than the raw value: the rate function turns the total into events per second and handles resets.

cards.q: A page fires whenever database CPU passes 80%, and half the pages need no action. Reframe it using the symptoms-versus-causes rule.
cards.a: CPU is a cause. Page on what users feel, such as error-budget burn rate or user-visible latency, and put CPU on the dashboard for diagnosis. Keep cause-based pages only for predictable exhaustion with no early symptom, such as a disk that will fill in four hours.

glossary.note: Tom Wilkie's three metrics for every service: requests per second, failures per second, and the latency distribution.
Brendan Gregg's checklist for every resource: how busy it is, how much work is queued because it cannot be served, and how many errors it reports.

sources.title: Prometheus docs, "Metric types"
sources.supports: counter (monotonic, resets to zero on restart), gauge, histogram (_bucket, _sum, _count) and summary definitions

sources.title: Prometheus docs, "Histograms and summaries"
sources.supports: histogram buckets aggregate across instances while summary quantiles cannot; averaging quantiles is 'statistically nonsensical'; quantile error bounded by bucket width; a boundary at the SLO threshold makes the share under it exact; recommendation to prefer native histograms

sources.title: Prometheus docs, "Query functions: histogram_quantile()"
sources.supports: the sum by (le) rate(...) form and the uniform-distribution (linear) interpolation within a bucket

sources.title: Prometheus docs, "Metric and label naming"
sources.supports: every unique label combination is a new time series; do not use labels for high-cardinality dimensions such as user ids or email addresses

sources.title: Prometheus docs, "FAQ: Why do you pull rather than push?"
sources.supports: reasons for pulling (run a monitoring instance on a laptop, tell when a target is down, inspect a target in a browser), the Pushgateway for cases where you must push, and the statement that pull versus push is not a major point

sources.title: prometheus/client_golang package docs, DefBuckets
sources.supports: the default histogram boundaries .005 to 10 seconds (11 boundaries) tailored to network-service response times

sources.title: Brendan Gregg, "The USE Method"
sources.supports: for every resource check utilisation, saturation and errors; definitions of the three terms; intended for early-stage performance investigation

sources.title: Grafana Labs blog, "The RED Method: How to Instrument Your Services" (report of Tom Wilkie's GrafanaCon talk)
sources.supports: Tom Wilkie created RED in 2015; Rate, Errors, Duration; RED as the four golden signals without saturation; USE for hardware-like resources; apply RED to every service so people can be on call for code they did not write

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 6 "Monitoring Distributed Systems" (written by Rob Ewaschuk)
sources.supports: the four golden signals; symptoms versus causes; every page should be urgent and actionable; prefer catching symptoms over causes; distributions rather than means

sources.title: Rob Ewaschuk, "My Philosophy on Alerting"
sources.supports: the essay's ideas form the foundation of the SRE book's monitoring chapter; alert on symptoms, keep causes on dashboards; the sparing exception for resources walking towards a cliff (quota, memory, disk)

sources.title: Prometheus docs, "Alerting" (practices)
sources.supports: alert on latency and errors as high in the stack as possible; page on latency at only one point in a stack; page on user-visible errors
